Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Having bowed his head to the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, who is together with Umā,
who is endowed with a digit [of power], who is beautiful, possessed of immeasurable splendor, praised, and the bestower of gifts;
Kārtikeya said:
O Supreme Lord, you have spoken of various mantras in this world that are wondrous, bestowing both spiritual perfection and liberation. Why do they not grant these fruits?
I have not heard of any *gāruḍa* [scripture] that provides immediate remedy;
for him, what is the best eye-remedy? It is the *amattaka* and the *saṃkara*.
The smooth account of the birth from the womb of the various classes of nāgas in their entirety,
the physical forms of all the nāgas, and the birth stories of the vyantaras.
The characteristics of the Grahas, Pakṣadis, Sāvās, and Sākinīs,
as well as those cruel Bālagrahas who, being merciless, cause affliction— [these are described here].
O Lord of Gods, tell me the description of those who create pits for women, as well as the characteristics of cow-slayers and of scorpions.
There are also various other malignant [creatures], such as *latākīṭa* and *lūtā*; fevers are said to be of many kinds, both curable and indeed incurable.
The yoga of knowledge, the initiation of action, and the characteristics of the mantras are, in brief,
the means for achieving the accomplishment of those who have been initiated.
The Gāruḍa, the Sūta, the Tantra, the Carma, and likewise the Vāda—
all that was previously unknown to me, O Lord of Gods.
Speak it yourself, O Mahādeva, you who grant fearlessness to the wretched.
The Lord said:
Listen, I shall explain to you in truth the supreme essence of the Tantra,
which was previously told to the Goddess and kept secret from others by me.
O Lord of Gods, the Gāruḍa, the science of mantras, and whatever supreme Siddhānta exists— all these are established [in this system], and it is proclaimed that they do not exist elsewhere.
The God who bestows all accomplishments, the giver of all knowledge,
and the granter of both worldly enjoyment and liberation— he is indeed the Lord of Causes for his devotees.
There is nothing in this world or the next that is devoid of him;
he is indeed Brahmā, he is Viṣṇu, he is Rudra, and he is Purandara.
He is Rudra, Soma, Sūrya, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
he is the station, the god of all gods, the all-pervading, both the transcendent and the immanent.
When the yogi becomes absorbed in that [state],
the practitioner of mantra attains accomplishment upon knowing it; there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*. The Lord said:
O child, in ancient times, the characteristics of the Gāruḍa [mantra] were both auspicious and inauspicious;
having understood that in its true essence, the wise man should thereafter commence his ritual action.
O child, I shall now describe, in brief and according to the truth, the characteristics of yakṣas, rākṣasas, grahas, and ḍākinīs.
Nāgas are said to be of two kinds; they are remembered as being divine and non-divine.
One should observe the four various classes separately.
Thus have the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras been described; now hear from me concerning the nature of the castes, both divine and non-divine, in their entirety.
The Brahmins were born from the peaks of Meru, and the Kṣatriyas were born there as well;
those who belong to the Vaiśya caste are the Nāgas born on Gandhamādana.
And the Śūdras who dwell on Mount Mandara are divine, appearing like Yāmas;
they are declared to be born of Brahmā and are wanderers of the intermediate space.
Likewise, others born of Rudra through the great-souled Kātyāyana,
as well as other Nāga kings and lords of the gods among the Nāga kings.
The divine form [of the deity] consists of eight aspects, beginning with Ananta and ending with Kulika;
they are indeed the planets, the nāgas, and the world-protectors, though they have been forgotten.
All of them, established by their own appointment and according to their will,
protect the entire world, pervading their respective stations.
Whosoever among them were born are described as both divine and non-divine; they dwell in the netherworld, the atmosphere, and on earth, being mind-born and able to assume any form at will.
Inconceivable beings wander upon the surface of the earth in the world of men;
others are said to be non-Vajras, and they are proclaimed to be non-Rudras.
The Brāhmaṇas are of white complexion, the Kṣatriyas are of red complexion,
the Vaiśyas are of yellow complexion, and the Śūdras are declared to be black.
And for all the serpents, there are four distinct classes;
they range through the three worlds, enjoying divine and non-divine pleasures and seats.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial flowers, those divine beings,
assuming forms at will, each remained separately in their own respective abodes.
Furthermore, I shall speak briefly of the inconceivable [mantras]; listen with diligence.
They are to be practiced on delightful mountains, in houses, or in hermitages.
In the delightful Mahāpadma lake, at the confluence of the garden and the serpent-king,
those serpents among the twice-born who dwell eternally in the places of cattle.
O Six-faced One, for Kṣatriyas, these are the six locations: at the crossroads, in the best of houses, at the gate of the enclosure wall, and at the archway.
In Gokula, Goṣṭha, Koṣṭhāra, and in the houses of the engine-hall,
the Vaiśyas dwell constantly in happiness in these five places.
Near water or in its midst, and within our forests,
these Śūdras constantly wander everywhere, from place to place.
The twice-born and the serpents eat wind, flowers, fruits, and leaves;
the Kṣatriyas eat only light, and the Vaiśyas eat frogs.
The Śūdras and all those who eat everything, as well as the Vyantaras born there,
a Brāhmaṇa should wander in the east and south, while a Kṣatriya should wander at midday.
A Vaiśya [should menstruate] on the third lunar day under the constellation Yāmya (Bharaṇī) in the afternoon; those of Śūdra birth,
as well as Vaiśyas, [should menstruate] between the constellations Savāṇa and Sarpī when she is in her season.
Their sexual union should take place during the period of the husband's menses;
she should not conceive a child during the four months of the rainy season.
O wise one, there are two hundred and forty eggs below;
they are indeed cooked by fire, of this there is no doubt regarding the eggs.
Those born in the month of Kārttika are exceedingly fierce, possessing potent poison;
they are red in color, swift in their venom, very large, and move rapidly with their coils.
Those born in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa are known to be stout yet short;
they have red eyes, possess little enjoyment, and are known to have mild venom.
The female snake protects [the offspring] for seven days once it has emerged from the egg;
but when the seven days have passed, it perishes by itself.
From that, three are produced: female, male, and the neuter;
O child, when the eggs have burst open, they become possessed of minds like those of the Salākāha bird.
Motionless and poison-free, they remain for twenty-one days;
then, in the third fortnight, their own names move.
Having uprooted the tops of the sugarcane, they gaze upon the solar disc.
From that time forward, the lords of serpents were born with venom;
in brief, those snakes bite in ten ways as they inflict their venom.
Terrified, insane, and tormented by hunger; overcome, and arrogant with the pride of poison; desiring food and offspring, he is intent on protecting his own place.
The ninth is indeed the sound *va*, while the tenth is impelled by the syllable *o*.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
Īśvara said:
Listen thus in brief, O dear one, from me who seeks the welfare of all the world:
fangs in the mouth of a serpent are said to be of eight kinds in this world.
Karālī, Kapālī, and Vāyavī as the third;
Dhūmrā, Krūrā, Ugrā, Bhīṣaṇī, and Viparītadhī.
That [teeth] is said to have eight fangs, while the ninth is known as Kāla.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord of Umā, what indeed is the name of the perception of time? In whom does it arise? And in which limb of the serpents does their poison reside?
The Lord said:
O child, on the palate of the serpent there is a mark shaped like a sprout;
from it the terrible poison is released, and for that reason she is known as Kālā.
But by the power of that nāga’s charm and amulet,
the poison that had fallen upon the bite then receded from the bodily constituents.
A bite may be of four kinds: punctured, pierced, torn, and lacerated;
the divine bite is distinct from these, and I shall describe their characteristics.
A bite by one [fang] is known as *ekadaṃśa*, and a bite by three [fangs] is *tridaṃśaka*.
That which is bitten by another [animal] after being bitten is *khaṇḍita*, while that which is gnawed without being bitten is *avalupta*.
If a wheel is seen extended on the left side and a single mark on the right, one should know it as "bitten by fear"; in that case, no poison is present.
O sons of Kṛtikā, when an enemy is seen approaching while dripping with saliva, that is the sign of one who is intoxicated by pride.
Where a bite is seen to be torn, smeared with saliva, and located between two punctures,
that bite of one afflicted by hunger shall be life-taking along with its venom.
Where many biting insects are seen, such as gadflies and ants,
they should be known as non-venomous, even though they bite one who has been stepped upon.
When many bites are seen that are characterized by a throbbing pain and a burning sensation,
one should recognize them as the bites of a venomous snake and treat them accordingly.
When a bite has two fangs that are straight and one that is curved,
the wise know that the poison in such a bite intended for feeding is slight.
When many saliva-drops have entered into the midst of the flesh,
one should then undertake the ritual action for those excessively biting insects.

If he has been bitten by two or three places by one following an old enmity, one should treat him with an ointment as described before; there is no doubt. One whose single bite becomes excessive in blood [should be treated likewise].
Whether it be a three-biter or a single-biter, one should know that it is impelled by time.
When the bite has the shape of a wheel, resembles a ripe jambu fruit,
is well-sweated, very painful, and has the appearance of an ariṣṭa fruit;
If one's own son, or one burnt by fire, should flow with excessive blood,
and an extremely intense pain arises at the base of the bite;
When one sees that region as white, or even devoid of color,
and it appears in such a form, then understand it to be the time of death.
Likewise,
a fracture of the jaw, or similarly of the palate, separation of the lower teeth from the gums, or even a fracture of the neck;
There is pain in the heart as well as in the sides, a burning sensation in the limbs, and agony;
urine and feces are discharged, and a breaking pain in the joints arises.
Thus, having seen such auspicious marks, there is no doubt that the time of death has arrived;
for even when being struck with a staff, no mark of the staff is visible.
If one's body hairs do not stand on end even when sprinkled repeatedly with cold water, one should know that person to be impelled by Time (Death).
If one does not see both the sun and moon, as well as two lamps, together with a bright light, then one should declare her destruction; she has reached the end, there is no doubt about this.
The two names should be reddish; no defect is found therein.
One should not speak of him who lives with his younger brother; [he is] the banner...?
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
The Lord said:
The fifth, the full moon, the eighth, and the fourteenth—these lunar days are indeed childless; so too are the constellations of Nidhana.
Kṛttikā, Śravaṇa, Mūla, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Maghā, the three Pūrvās, Citrā, and likewise Aśleṣā.
One should avoid these inauspicious activities during the two *ṛkṣa* periods;
likewise, one should avoid the *daṃśa* periods of the lunar mansions, as well as the times when the sun is eclipsed or obscured by clouds.
When the vital points (marmas), the locations (sthānas), and the conjunctions (samudāyas) are all absent,
and if these [inauspicious] signs are seen, then success is not found.
O Lord, these substances are located in the throat, in the middle of the hands, in the joints,
on the lower lip, in the head, in the middle of the trunk, in the eyes, and likewise in the anus.
In the vital points (*marmas*)— namely, the head, the neck, and likewise the palate— these are the locations where,
if bitten, one does not survive.
In a garden, at an old well, under a banyan tree, in a city, at an aralu tree,
at a withered tree, in a cremation ground, at a triple-junction, and at crossroads.
In an empty house, on its peak, in temples,
and at *śigru*, *śleṣmātaka*, *kharjūra*, and *vinītaka* trees.
Those humans who are bitten in the position of the cattle,
or at midday, during the two twilights, at midnight, or at the end of the night, do not survive.
For these times are always unfavorable; one should observe the specific characteristics of the time. I shall now declare those that are unbound, as well as those that are very firm and auspicious.
Everything—whether incurable or indeed curable—is perceived as ripe [for death];
one situated at a distance utters cries and groans again and again.
Or one who causes the shedding of human blood, or one with hands like the staffs of nooses;
one who eats the food of those who are terrified, distressed, or weary; and one who mounts asses, camels, or buffaloes.
One whose limbs are covered in black garments, who moves about while smeared with red lead,
who is worshipped by low-born people, who is joyful yet wicked, who speaks harsh words, or who acts like fire— such a person is a *kudvasta*.
Anointed with oil, smeared with blood, covered in waves, ashes on his body,
red and sharp, a wretched man, a white mendicant.

One who holds a scale, one with a hand missing, or one with an extra limb; one whose nose is cut off, one whose staff is broken, one who is burnt, one who is crying out, or one who has a weapon in his hand.
And for whomsoever a maiden serves as a messenger, she likewise becomes his consecrated consort.
By these [means], one does not achieve success; one is excluded from all ritual acts.
I shall describe other auspicious [methods] by which success is produced:
one who has complete limbs, possesses intelligence, wears white garments, and has an excellent covering.
With white flowers, his limbs unanointed, one-pointed in mind, he is a meditator.
One who speaks firm words like nectar, free from all diseases,
[should worship] with flowers, fruits, leaves, sprouts, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
He does not cause the rivers to overflow; he possesses excellent vision and a steady seat;
he is free from weapons and punishment regarding the laws of his own class and kind.
It should be known that when there is a wind-related tremor, [the mantras] bestow all accomplishments once they have been extracted;
however, one should avoid the patient's own kinsmen, lineage, and body.
When such a person has been carried away, that time is impelled by destiny;
it is likewise improper for vultures, owls, dogs, and cats [to be present].
Having seen a jackal, a donkey, a camel, a buffalo, or a pig;
or seeing washermen, insects, one wearing saffron robes, or one dressed in yellow or deep red garments.
If a physician sets out on his journey and observes these omens,
his work there will not succeed, unless the tree itself should be Arka.
I do not take to heart words that are unspoken, nor those that are harsh;
likewise, [I do not dwell on one who is] terrified, lost, well-off, joined, devoted, or ruined.
And Viṣṇu heard those words: "He has been consumed by his own [deeds], slain, destroyed, departed, gone, fallen, and fainted."
One should avoid words that are disjointed, violent, divisive, bluish (morose), or abandoned, as well as those concerning raw flesh. One should speak with great care.
Then the king, seeing the brahmin Śiva— who was joyful and borne by a bull, a cow, an elephant, and a full water-jar— along with his yogins, was delighted.
The earth, a hand, wine, or even a canopy, a banner, and a chowrie;
a woman of beautiful appearance with all her limbs complete, gold, gems, coral, and pearls.
Raw meat, honey-meat, or likewise curd that has been removed [from the milk],
white flowers, dūrvā grass, fresh sandalwood, and gorocanā.
For one who hears the sound of the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and the deliberation upon the scriptures of accomplishment (*siddhi*),
there is success without a doubt.
O child, the procedure for examining the patient is extended by means of the causes (nidāna);
that is declared as the "Compendium" (saṃgraha) in both the section on examination and the compendium itself.
One determines the cause according to its actual meaning through definitive certainty;
therefore, they call it the "nidāna" (source), for by means of it, there is a gathering together in the compendium.
When medical treatment is to be performed, it must be done according to reality by means of mantras; otherwise, there will be a concealment of the disease due to the failure of the remedy.
This has been told in this tantra, O Skanda, in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
Kārttikeya said:
O Lord, O Maheśvara, you previously stated that your body consists of seven constituents; how, then, O Lord, can it be known through its transformations?
The Lord said:
Listen with one-pointed mind, O son, to that which is situated within the three realms; it is like a drop of oil fallen upon water, yet in the state of inversion.
In this way, the poison residing in the body increases upon reaching the blood;
it becomes twofold in the skin and fourfold in the flesh.
In pitta it should be known as having eight qualities, while phlegm (śleṣman) has sixteen;
in vāta it is said to have twenty qualities, and marrow (majjā) possesses thirty.
When it has reached the place of the marrow, the poison is said to be without guile;
O child, one should recognize the poison that has entered the bodily constituents even by its distinct characteristics.
One should not apply medicine to the mouth of a wicked person, O Skanda; when the poison has entered one's own body, one should observe the symptoms of its form.
In this regard, I shall explain the non-harming (*agarda*) by which happiness is attained:
the root of the *arka* plant, *apāmārga*, *priyaṅgu*, and likewise *candana*.
One should administer a drink and an ointment; by that, well-being is attained.
However, if the poison does not subside once that treatment has been performed, [further measures must be taken].
And you, having gone from that place, are born again among those who are passionate;
having reached the place of the passionate, one does not perceive their true forms.
There is intense pain in the head, the eyes are filled with tears, and the gums bleed;
the palate becomes swollen, shaped like a ripe jambu fruit.
One should recognize those symptoms which appear when the poison has settled in the blood;
one must provide a remedy for that and should not neglect the victim who has been bitten.
Usīra, sandalwood, priyaṅgu, saffron, and nakha should be given as a drink and an ointment; from that, happiness is attained.
Even when this has been done, O child, if the poison does not recede,
it leaves the location of the blood and takes its stand in the location of the flesh.
I shall describe its forms; listen now with disciplined vows.
One perceives the entire world there as being of golden-yellow color and exceedingly beautiful.
The limbs burn excessively and throb again and again;
he in whom these symptoms appear has poison located in the flesh.
One should administer an antidote for him by which well-being is attained:
the essence of honey, along with asafoetida, saffron, and likewise rohiṇī.
One should administer a drink or an ointment; from that, well-being is attained.
Even by this method, however, if the poison does not recede—
Having completely left the location of the flesh, it resides in the location of the bile;
even while situated in the location of the bile, one should observe its various forms.
Regarding the passage beginning with "he becomes yellow-colored" and so forth, or alternatively: his complexion becomes fair, and his eyes become yellow; of this there is no doubt.
O child, when one has consumed poison, this medicinal formulation comes into being;
therein, however, medicine must be administered so that well-being is attained.
One should administer a drink consisting of kuṣṭha, fresh ginger, triphalā, sandalwood, and ghee; by this, well-being is attained.
Now, when that treatment has been performed, if that poison is not warded off,
it bypasses the bile and remains in the phlegm.
Even there, I shall describe the physical signs by which they may be known:
the mouth emits a foul odor and saliva flows profusely.
In one's own presence, as well as during sleep, excessive food does not undergo digestion.
One should observe these signs when poison has reached an improper location;
having identified it, one should [treat] the head of the arrow-head, which is truly terrible and most cruel.
One should administer treatment there with medicinal substances in brief:
namely, *kaṭukā*, *sahā*, leaves, as well as *rājaghoṣa* and *ātakī*.
One should administer triphalā, candraka, citra, and kuṇḍavāruṇī as a drink and as an ointment; thereby, well-being is attained.
Then, when the ritual has been performed in this manner, if the poison does not recede,
it abandons the seat of phlegm and moves into the seat of wind.
I shall describe its characteristics by which they truly conquer;
the limbs contract and the complexion becomes discolored.
One who suffers from vomiting, fainting, and loss of consciousness—
these are the symptoms of one whose poison has entered the vital air (vāyu).
For this, one should prepare the following medicine by which well-being is attained:
the eyes of a pigeon, yellow orpiment, and realgar.
One should administer the drink as an ointment; from that, happiness is attained.
Furthermore, other substances [are also effective]; all [of these] ward off poison.
And by the mere scent of these, all those serpents, though arrogant with poison,
become devoid of venom, being utterly bewildered by the power of the substance.
Having always anointed themselves, children seize a snake;
they play with it as if it were a toy, and thus they do not fear the serpents.
Now, if one should be bitten through negligence and overcome by the poison,
[one should apply] śirīṣa seed, tagara, and likewise red mālākīṇī.
One should collect Vyādhighāta, Madhusāra, Kuṣṭha, Tagara,
Sirikarṇikā, and Mākṣika, and drink them together in equal proportions.
One should saturate these substances— goat, boar,
mongoose, and peacock— with the bile of a cat.
Having made a paste with wine and applied it, one should cause it to fall upon him;
all the nāgas will submit, for there is no need for further deliberation in this matter.
This is the remedy for him who possesses great splendor and great heroism and prowess;
it [overcomes] the fierce yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as the piśācas and ḍākinīs.
There are quartan fevers and others that arise from the combination of two substances.
All poisons perish like serpents before Garuḍa;
therefore, having understood the course of Time, one should perform one's action.
Kārttikeya said:
Tell me truly the time by which the mixtures are exhausted;
O Lord, they do not arise together, but rather they arise individually.
The Lord said:
Time is said to be of two kinds, according to the division into gross and subtle;
the gross is established by the planets and stars, while the subtle arises from the most excellent [internal] occurrences.
O child, I shall explain that in the Tantra in brief, but not in detail;
by means of lines drawn horizontally and upwards, and arranged according to their numerical counts.
A wise person should not make a single square five hundred years old;
one should place the planetary diagram there, beginning with the planets and followed by the nāgas.
Those who are *grahas* are indeed *nāgas*, and those who are *nāgas* are known as *grahas*.
They say that Takṣaka is the king, and Kārkoṭa is called Soma.
Śubha is declared to be Śuṅgi; Mahāpadma is called Sukra;
Saṃkhapāla is to be known as [the next]; these seven Nāgas are the planets in order.
The eighth is Kulika, the Naga-Rahu, who is a cruel planet;
he is designated as Kala, the Kulika of terrible form.
One should place the seven nāgas in the squares, arranging them again and again;
beginning with Ananta, they are situated in their respective places according to the guardians of the directions.
With arms reaching half a watch, seven swords, and moving exceedingly fast— having attacked Yama for half a watch, I see Kulika somewhere.
It burns swiftly at its arising, constantly within the joints;
thirty breaths are divided by three, and then again divided by three in succession.
O child, this is the measure of time established for whichever [planet] is situated at its rising;
it is always established in the movement of the Sun, and specifically at the rising of Karkaṭa.
In the middle of the victorious half [of the month], Kulikā always moves through the seven great [nāgas];
furthermore, at the rising of Padma, Saṃkhapāla and Mahāpadma [move].
The formidable Kulika, ever constant, partakes [of the offering] at the three times of day.
At the rising of Kujā in the half-pada of Padmā, there is indeed the rising of Saṃkhapāla;
the rising of Kulika is to be known in this very manner—of this there is no doubt.
And when half of the Buddha's lifespan has elapsed, the arising of the Kulika occurs;
that time is at all times a thief of life and vitality.
There may be danger from Padma, Saṃkhapāla, and Takṣaka;
these [planets] are declared to be harmful to the Kulika when they occur on a Saturday.
Even for Sukra, it is well known that when Saṃkhapāla bestows [his influence],
one bitten by a snake shall not live, nor shall one do so under Kulika.
Just as there is a twofold rising of Kulika along with Niścara,
so too is it for Saṃkhapāla at the time of his [rising], and likewise for Karkoṭaka.
The time is declared to be malefic according to the positions of the planets in the planetary wheel;
one who is bitten during the risings of Kulika shall not live, even if cut by a weapon.
Or even if one has stumbled.
No one should administer poison, nor should they apply medicines;
likewise, one must observe the shadow of time, the time itself, the Sukra-pati, and the planetary aspects.
O Skanda, within the interval of thirty breaths, three periods (velās) are proclaimed;
whatever form the time may take, its shadow shall likewise be so.
One bitten during the Cakra period survives, and even one bitten during Chāyā survives;
however, for one bitten at the time of Savya, his life comes to an end.
Among these, the gross has been fully described; now learn the subtle [wind].
It is Svacchanda and Vāmadeva that then flows within the self.
One who stands there, though unfortunate, may ask, for success will certainly be attained;
whether the forms are non-terrible, terrible, or gentle, they are [realized] by means of the syllable.
If, having become intent on yoga, one asks about two things that carry one's own welfare, then one should know that death is near; there is no need for further deliberation here.
Wherever she may be situated, I ask [you] while facing south;
having gone to that very place of assembly, by means of its arising.
The Aghora person is to be entered into the divine abode, yet it does not come [to me].
At the time when Vāma and Aghora are equal, one should speak of the neuter body.
Having understood the movement of the deity, one should then determine its strength and weakness:
gentle rites should be performed when it is in a gentle state, and middling rites when it is in a non-terrible (aghorā) state.
This has been fully declared as the secret of secrets, one's own supreme mantra. Now I shall speak of another arising, namely that of the pentad of kalās.
Likewise, that suffering and even death are of the nature of *rajas*;
five, five, and five times over, they are to be offered to Gaṇapati in the *Svarodaya*.
And the group of five beginning with *ā* is likewise remembered;
one should arrange these long vowels in their proper sequence by means of six vertical and six horizontal lines drawn in succession.
One should arrange fifteen squares in successive order for the lunar days (tithis):
Trayodaśī, Trayodaśī-saṃjñā, Guvāsā, and Pīḍa.
The three deaths are known as the lunar days (tithis), beginning with the first (pratipad) in due order; [the lords of these are] Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.
O Lord, these indeed are to be known as the digits (kalās): the son of Kṛttikā,
Revatī, Ādri, Mṛga, and Anāśa, from the asterism (ṛkṣa) and then from Time (kāla).
For the others, exactly five constellations each are proclaimed;
these are the risings of Caitra and the following months, one for each period of time.
Twelve days and two months are to be understood separately for each;
however, the first portion of the name remains as the digit that abides within the Linga.
To that person who is afflicted by disease, oppressed by planetary influences, or tormented by spirits, he grants the [proper] lunar day,
the tithi, as well as the weekday, the asterism, and even the month.
A name must be preceded by its arising; it is thus, and not otherwise.
This unprecedented [teaching], known as the "Arising of the Kola," has been told by me to you.
One should not give this to anyone who does not know it; it must be guarded with great effort.
These are the colors of Mahendra, Varuṇa, Agni, and likewise Vāyu.

One should know that there are four types [of mantras] according to their means of accomplishment and the practitioner: those of Mahendra (Tāntrika), Vāruṇa (Mantra), and Āvarṇa (Yoga); the first letter of the name is always [the seed-syllable].
He who is bitten by a snake, or even one facing death from fire or demons,
shall live if he stands before the Puṣpadhvaja [liṅga], which is entirely covered with a white cloth.
But one standing at a distance should ascertain whether the bitten person is alive by means of auspicious sounds produced by a woman.
The drum sounds for the practice of the great festival while the mantra-dancer dances;
it should not be understood that one who is far away lives when bitten by a snake.
Thus one should examine the person, and then one should commence the ritual action;
this is declared as the Kālacakra, by which [beings] are known according to reality.
Having examined [the subject] through various forms and brilliant causal factors—
thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
The Lord said:
Now I shall further explain the five principles as they truly exist:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
Kṣi and the others are of five colors; these are the lords of the maṇḍalas. Yūṃ, yūṃ, yāṃ, jāya, vijāya, kathā, and diśi are the expressive mantras.
Distinguished by long vowels, excluding the neuter [vowels],
one should assign the six limbs of Śiva as proclaimed, according to their respective order.
The placement [of mantras] situated in their respective locations— namely the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and likewise the weapon— bestows the complete accomplishment of all ritual actions.
Likewise, the fire (ra) and the abode (va) are joined with the sixth vowel (ū),
conjoined with the upper crescent and the bindu, and differentiated by the supreme and the non-supreme (Parā and Aparā).

This is indeed the extraction of Śiva; one should pierce it with the syllable *ra* (repha) and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the true method upon the heart, the palm of the hand, and the body.
When unrecited, it performs the ritual action; when recited, it bestows all perfections.
It is joined with the fourth-born [vowel] and is extended across four squares.
The earth, the vajra, and the deities are yellow in color;
in the center, it is joined with a lotus and a cool half-moon.
A triangle joined with svastikas, always filled with rays of knowledge;
this is the Agni-maṇḍala, employed for the rites of stobha, snāpana, and dīpana.
One should meditate upon the wind [element] as having the appearance of crushed collyrium, perfectly circular like the moon, stainless,
possessing sharp speed, and terrifying.
One should meditate upon the sky as having the appearance of waves of milk, possessing the luster of pure crystal,
and flooding the entire world with nectar.
O King, Vāsuki and Saṃkhapāla are situated in the earthly circle;
one should place Karkoṭaka and Padmanābha in the western [circle].
The knower of mantras should always join Āgneya and Ananta with Kulika;
likewise, Takṣaka and Mahāpadma [should be joined] with Vyāsa in the Vāyavya maṇḍala.
The Pārthiva Kṣatriyas are to be known as marked with a red thunderbolt;
the Kṛṣṇas are Vāruṇa Nāgas, distinguished by the auspicious lotus.
The Brahmins are produced from the fire of their own weapons and are marked with the *svastika*;
the Vaiśyas are said to be born from the wind and are adorned with a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) on the crown of the head.
One should place the five elements, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger,
in both direct and reverse order.
And on the thumb is Jayajaṃ, and the Nāgas are stationed in front.
The elements from the heart up to Śiva are established in sequence starting from the little finger;
thereafter, Śiva pervades both hands as well.
First, one should perform the placement of the *tṛtva* [mantras] upon the joints of the thumbs and fingers; then again, the placement of the elements (*bhūta*) and likewise the limbs of Śiva.
Beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, combined with the left [hand],
one should subsequently pervade Śiva within both hands.
The procedure for the worship of other deities has been declared among all mantras;
indeed, the first syllable of a name is prescribed as its mantra.
The cause for the presence of the mantras of the eight nāga kings is the state of being moistened by the end of the [vowel] class, illuminated by the vowels *ā*, *ī*, and *ṅja*.
O Deva, one should place the syllable *tṛtatvam* upon the head of all; then, preceded by the five elements, one should cast [the mantra] in sequence as *kṣipa aṃ svāhā*.
O Garuḍa, the *pādya* [offering] shall become manifest as the accomplisher of all rites;
having first performed the *kara-nyāsa*, one should then perform the *vinyāsa* upon the body.
The wise one should contemplate the blazing Praṇava, the cause of purification;
thereafter, he should contemplate the seed-syllable *pav*, which is most excellent and of the nature of nectar.
Having performed this nourishment in this manner, one should contemplate [the earth] upon one's own head;
one should place the earth, radiant like molten gold, at the feet.
The wise man should place this blessed Earth within his own body— she who is strewn with all worlds and well-accumulated by the Lokāloka mountain.
Then one should join the *āpaṃ* [mudrā], not exceeding the knees in the interval;
one should meditate on the earth as being of a dark-green color and twice the size of oneself.

Having placed within the space between the navel and the neck the blazing family of garlands of flames, which consists of the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā and is mobile, one should visualize a triangular mandala.
One should meditate upon [the deity] who resembles crushed collyrium, who stands pervading everything, who is situated at the crown of one's own head, and who is doubly fierce and terrifying.
Situated at the very tip of the crest-lock is the divine, possessing the luster of pure crystal;
it is the Great Space, the standard of measure, all-pervasive, and like nectar.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the *nāgas* in their proper order— namely,
the letters *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *uṃ* joined with the nasal bindu—
one should then apply the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*) and subsequently meditate upon the mandala.
If the wise one has described the form of this mandala, [then...]
There, at the time of performing the rite, one who knows the ritual procedure should contemplate its color;
it has wings like those of a bird and a beak, and is adorned with eight serpents.
One should indeed constantly meditate upon Tākṣya in all things, whether stationary or moving, and among poisons;
likewise, against the planets, spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and ḍākinīs.
Having separated Śiva from the Nāgas, one should place him within one's own body;
this is declared to be the twofold placement (nyāsa) for both the elemental beings and the serpents.
Having understood this according to its true meaning, one should then commence the ritual action;
[namely] the self, the reality, and likewise knowledge, in the sequence of the Śiva-reality.
Having first offered the three *tattvas*, the practitioner of the Śiva-mantra [should place them] thereafter upon the joints of the fingers, just as they are in the body, so too in the deity.
Having first performed the placement of the deities upon the body (dehanyāsa), one should likewise perform the internal worship,
[visualizing] the root-tube (kaṇḍa), the stalk (nāla), and the lotus, as well as dharma, jñāna, and the other [qualities].
One should worship with the final letter of the [corresponding] class, distinguished by the second vowel;
O child, [the syllable] "kvaum" for the Karmikā [is] joined with the letter "ra" on the head.
The letters *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* are in the fifth group;
likewise, the eighth group consists of those [letters] from the east up to the northeast, placed in sequence upon the eight petals.
Starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, one should assign the sixteen vowels to the [deities] beginning with Keśava;
then the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā are declared, and thereafter one should perform the placement of the three principles (tattvas).
The image should be seated there, and above that, the body of Śiva;
one should worship the Lord together with his limbs (attendants) there, preceded by the ritual of the *karṇikā*.
One should place Earth on the western petal, Water situated in the north, Fire on the southern petal, and join Wind with the east.

In that [rite], the practitioner should indeed worship up to the vessel, beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra);
thereafter, the practitioners should worship the limbs of Śiva and the abodes (dhāman).
The Heart mantra of Agni should be worshipped in the southeast, and the Head in the northeast;
one should place the Crest in the southwest and conquer the Armor in the northwest.
The weapon (astra) should be placed on the exterior, and the eye (netra) situated to the north;
one should always worship the seed-syllables (bījas) at the tips of the jewel-studded petals.
The eight [nāgas], beginning with Ananta and ending with Kulika, are situated in the sequence of the nāgas;
from the east up to the southeast, they are the destroyers of obstacles for those born under the lunar mansions.
Having pierced this [lotus] with the lotuses of his hands within the heart-lotus, which is the mandala of fire—
this is the procedure prescribed for both the daily and occasional rites.
One should meditate upon the Self as twofold: as one whose form is at will and incomparable, and as the one who causes the entire world to be created and withdrawn.
A garland of flames [extends] from all of them as far as the world of Brahmā;
[it has] three eyes and a beautiful form. (p.
Ten-armed, with a face like the moon, tawny-eyed, and holding a trident in his hand.

At the time of performing ritual actions, one should always contemplate oneself as Bhairava, who has terrifying fangs, is exceedingly fierce, possesses three eyes, bears the moon upon his crest, and is the destroyer of all malevolent spirits.
If the Tārkya [fire] is for the purpose of destroying the Nāgas, it possesses terrible prowess;
its two feet rest upon skulls, and its wings pervade the quarters.
The seven heavens are his chest, and the cosmic egg is situated at his throat;
Śiva contemplates him as extending from Rudra down to the level of a blade of grass.
Sadāśiva resides within the crest-lock, as indeed do the three powers;
Parāparā herself is directly manifest, while Tārkṣya pervades the forest.
He has three eyes and a fierce form, yet he is the destroyer of the poison that destroys the Nagas;
he is praised for his terrifying appearance, possessing a body that is the very form of Garuda.
The supreme practitioner should meditate upon [the deity] blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction;
having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), whatever he may contemplate in his mind, that shall come to pass.
That [suffering] would be bearable for him alone, or indeed it becomes like Garuḍa;
likewise, the pretas, bhūtas, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas [are overcome].
By the sight of him, quartan fevers and other such ailments are destroyed. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
The Lord said:
Henceforth, I shall explain the stationary and moving sources of poison;
having observed the signs upon the body of the patient, one may discern their auspicious or inauspicious nature.
If one does not see the reflection of one's own shadow in a mirror, in a drop of water, in a sword, or likewise in ghee or oil, one should always avoid that patient.
O child, in the case of every victim who has been bitten, one should observe this very sign and reflect upon it:
for one who has been sprinkled with cold water, there shall never be any horripilation.
When one is being struck with a staff, the king of staffs does not arise;
when there is a cutting, blood flows from him and his head-hairs fall away.
Behold these forms, that object of knowledge impelled by time; recognize these auspicious signs through their collective appearance.
Or rather, let the mind be directed toward a festival; wherever it is, success is not far off.
For one who sees a beautiful person approaching, even if that beautiful person remains at a distance, [it brings auspiciousness].
Having first performed the protection of the vital breath (*jīvarakṣā*), one should then commence the ritual action (*karma*).
In the center of the heart is a white, eight-petaled, and most beautiful lotus.
The life-force (jīva) situated within the letter *ṭha*, well-conjoined with the letters of the name,
is placed in the middle of the letter *e* within a lotus inside the cavity of a half-moon.
One should place the syllable *ṭha* at the throat, which consists of nectar above;
then again, the four yellow *vajriṇīs* in the sky above and below.
O bridegroom, O bride, at the outset, for the protection of the seed, whether it be written or even merely contemplated, this shall protect it; of this there is no doubt.
Having placed the thumb upward, one should meditate on the earth, which possesses the luster of gold; at the time of paralyzing, that Kulikā, having been stepped upon, becomes motionless.
One should meditate upon that second syllable of Varuṇa, which pervades the entire universe,
as being situated within the center of a lotus and resting upon a half-moon.
One should move the threatening gesture (tarjanī) joined with the seed-syllable once, one after another;
by that, all poison, whether stationary or mobile, becomes neutralized.
The letter *ra* consists of one hundred and eight [syllables]; it is a triangle surrounded by svastikas.
At the time of the *stobha*, it is designated as the middle finger.

The family of Jvālāmālā is red; it is established as the seed-syllable of Vāyu, situated within the belly of the Fire-god (Purandara), joined with the Bindu, and possessing fierce speed and a terrifying nature.
One should always cast it into the midst for the purpose of attraction, as well as for running and leaping;
it is also used in battle against poisons, planetary influences, and the like, wherever one may find it pleasing.
One should contemplate the fifth [syllable], the supreme immutable (paramākṣara), resembling pure crystal,
raining down streams of nectar upon the three places.
By placing [the mantra] at the head, heart, and navel, and drawing in the essence from the very end,
one renders the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, free from poison.
Now, the ritual action that ought to be performed for the happiness of men [is accomplished] by casting [the dice] five times, both in direct and reverse order.
Without recitation, there is no accomplishment regarding poisons, spirits, or fevers;
by mere remembrance, one performs the rite of the greatly powerful Vainateya.
At the beginning and the end, one should first [place] the first [syllable], while the remaining ones are according to their own nature;
having formed a casket with the earth, one should place the ten vajras all around.
All those [trees], both immovable and movable, were overshadowed by this tree; it was designated as *staṃsama*,
and no other is capable of shaking it.
The first seed-syllable is dissolved and placed in the second position;
the second is placed in the first position; and the remainder are situated within the nature of the end.
When it has become a drop, when it has become a drop, one should contemplate [the deity] in the form of a cloud upon the crown of the head,
raining down with a great torrent, cooling, and moving along the vital breath.
By means of the ritual application residing in the *apamārjīkara* [mantra],
one quickly renders a person afflicted by poison free from venom, even if bitten by Takṣaka himself.
Having agitated the *tūrya* vessel with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, the knower of mantras will certainly cause the *vardhanī* or the jar to overflow.
By sprinkling ponds, wells, and tanks one hundred times with this consecrated water,
they become free from poison in an instant through bathing, drinking, and immersion.
The seed-syllable of fire (ra) is erased, and the element of earth (la) is situated there;
having placed it at the beginning of the word for fire (vahni), one should recite: "daha pacasva" (burn, cook).
One should cause [the victim] to be tormented with a thousand verses while afflicted by molasses, salt,
and poison; standing in one's own city, by means of the mantra ending in *phaṭ*, one makes him run and leap about.
But that which has fallen from the fourth bath remains in the place occupied by the earthly element.
Making the first [syllable] *vāyava*, one should contemplate "go, go";
then, having elided the fifth, one should place the first [syllable] there.
One should meditate upon the first seed-syllable as flooding [the body];
it is taught that this brings about the expulsion of poison for beings afflicted by venom.
It destroys burning fever, colic, fainting, and headaches;
it likewise eliminates all diseases as well as various kinds of poison.
Earth and water are established in duality;
together with this, there is [the element] fire, which is established as a single name along with wind.
It effects stimulation for one situated on the five staffs; there is no doubt about this. It is located in the city of Pṛthivīnilamakāsāṃsakīya (?).
One who has been punished a hundred times should be struck with the Mañcū weapon;
he should be struck with the force of an incoming arrow and with that which is discharged from the heart.
Having consecrated with mantras a piece of earth joined with *kokosa* held in the hand,
one who stands at a distance may release a seizing spirit (*graha*) by touching [the patient] with it.
By rubbing [the body] with this very [mantra], one will become happy, [freeing oneself] from spider-bites, donkey-bites, eruptions, the pain of scorpions and the like.
The letter *kṣa* ending in a visarga, mounted upon the fire-vowel (*r*), endowed with the three vowels *a*, *a*, and *aḥ*,
situated within the city of wind and fire, possesses a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
When [the breath] is placed upon the feet, heart, or head, it causes intense throbbing and distress;
the patient is afflicted by quartan fevers, nāgas, and ḍākinīs.
One should paralyze them; of this there is no doubt—even those who revile the Brahmins, or a city or a house that has been defiled by fierce planetary spirits.
Having meditated upon it as enveloped in garlands of flames and kindled by this practice,
a malevolent spirit or even a serpent, seeing it, perishes in fear.
The first two [syllables] are devoid of the letter *ra* and adorned with the nasal bindu;
furthermore, specifically, the third remains in that same state.
One should meditate on the deity situated upon a lotus at the crown of the head, white in appearance and having the nature of nectar, flooding that afflicted person.
It quickly causes an irritation with the fist and poison;
it also knows the afflictions of spiders and burns, as well as eruptive boils and the *gardabha* [eruption].
May she protect from the pain of spear-wounds and the sting of scorpions;
by her mere remembrance, may she remove disease, poisons, and constant afflictions from afar.
The best of practitioners who remembers this application for seventy [days] will experience neither death, nor old age, nor even disease.
When contemplated upon the three locations—the heart, the mouth, and likewise the head—it removes all diseases; what need is there to mention those afflicted by poisons?
One who has consumed poison should meditate upon that very [mantra] situated within the seed-syllable of Vāyu, encircled by the wind, and endowed with the color of a bumblebee.
Whichever limb the best of physicians places [the pulse] upon the patient,
that limb of his moves when it is located at half [the distance].
The knower of the ritual procedure likewise causes the vessels to be washed and cleansed;
by this very method, he causes the vessels to be rinsed.
That is the supreme seed-syllable, the performer of many wonders;
it is the destroyer of planetary fevers and the cause of the destruction of all evils.

In all three intermediate periods, [one should perform the rite] under the asterisms of Revatī, Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Aśvinī, Puṣya,
and likewise Rohiṇī.
In a mother’s house, or in a house, at a triple-way junction or a quadruple-way junction,
at an old well or a pond, and at the confluences of rivers;
On the eighth lunar day, the king’s wife should then bathe [the deity] at midday in a solitary tree, a cremation ground, or even in a temple of the god.
One who has lost a son [should bathe] at Putragā, one who has lost a mother at Mātugo-tīrtha, a queen at the confluence (saṃgama), and one whose children have died at Mṛtaputrikā.
A woman who performs malevolent magic (abhicāra) is to be executed by crows in an old well, and in lotus ponds; likewise, a man devoid of semen is to be executed there.
One should diligently bathe her at the confluence of the Śiva-temple;
the preceptor, being fully perfected, [should likewise bathe her] with two clean white garments.
Measuring eight cubits, or even four cubits,
it should be square with four doors and adorned with archways beautified by colored powders.
One should cause various offerings (bali) to be made, consisting of food and drink, sacrificial gifts, and a garland of flowers that beautifies the formidable peak created by the ascetic Candra.
Having drawn the mandala that fulfills all desires with three lines—
the colors being white, red, and very black, in sequence from the outside to the inside.
Īśa, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are known as the presiding deities of the Rajasī [line].
Within the mandala, for the sake of enjoyment, one should perform the Svapana-maṇḍapa rite.
Adorned with colors to a measurement of four cubits, it is beautified by forms;
the kalaśas for Akāla-sūla are eight in number, according to the measurement of four [cubits].
[The vessels] should be joined with mango sprouts, wrapped in cloths,
accompanied by gold, dūrvā grass, medicinal herbs, and fragrances.
Having taken earth from both banks of a river, from the root of a nimba tree,
and from an anthill— one should place these in the first jar.
Having placed cow dung in the second [vessel], one should place fragrant substances in the third;
gold and silver in the fourth, and all medicinal herbs in the fifth.
In the sixth [kalaśa], all the tīrthas; in the seventh, the seven Mothers;
and in the eighth kalaśa, Saṃkara together with the Mothers.
Thereafter, one should consecrate those [images] with one hundred and eight mantras,
using well-perfumed scents and flowers.
One should worship the peaceful Śiva together with the Mothers within the mandala;
by this procedure, the practitioner of mantra should cause the consecration to be bestowed.
A woman who has previously borne stillborn children may give birth to a living son;
likewise, whether it be a woman or even a man, one who has not conquered [the senses] may attain victory.

By this very [rite], one is released from all constraints— the fault caused by malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) through the employment of mantras, medicinal herbs, rituals, and so forth— and from the effects of curses.
The maiden, though difficult to wed, sings beautifully and obtains an excellent husband;
even for those wicked children afflicted by the seizing of planets, the gods provide relief.
One endowed with all the [necessary] qualities should always perform this rite;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor consisting of a city, a village, or a market town.
Or [he may give] elephants, horses, chariots, or vehicles;
crowns, earrings, bracelets, necklaces, armlets, and various garments.
Or by whomsoever the Guru is robbed of wealth, grain, or gold.
When he is enraged, the deities and likewise the Mothers are satisfied;
furthermore, the vidyās become effective during the consecration.
Oṃ raiṃ hauṃ ruṃ vaṣaṭ!
Consecration, many times nailed within the womb: Oṃ ṣūṃ kṣa śrī svāhā!
By this, there is consecration for a man at the end of the menstrual flow; Oṃ Śrīṃ Layastathā.
But at the end of the menses, one should cause the consecration of women to be performed by Sanandā.
Oṃ caiṃ hauṃ svāhā.

With this, once it has been secured by the *kīlana* rite, one should always perform the consecration of the womb (*garbhābhiṣeka*). For its nourishment, however, [one uses] *yojī*; or else, if it is dead, the seed (*vusya*) falls as *vaṃ*.
Oṃ saṃ phaṭ svāhā.
In case of doubt, one should strike the child with mustard seeds or *rakṣata* (protective substances);
if the child remains silent, it will die, but if it cries, it will certainly live.
Thus ends the chapter on consecration in the Kriyākālaguṇottara.
Īśvara said:
I shall now explain, according to the truth, the treatment for complications arising from childbirth:
cirā, atiktaka, āriṣṭa, bhadramusta, and sandalwood.
One should also cook oil with the bark of *spatapaṇī*;
this is highly recommended for massage and is excellent for destroying all fevers.
Cirā, atiktā, rodhra, balā, atibalā, as well as sāliparṇī, pṛṣṭiparṇī, saptaparṇī, and tvacā;
Grind this finely and cook it; it wards off all fevers. One should administer it as nasal drops (nasya), for drinking, and as an ointment for the limbs.
The leaves of the *asvattha*, the leaf of the *eraṇḍa* and *śīrṣa*,
combined with the juice of *saptaparṇī*, used for bathing, destroy fever.
Aṣṭīmadhuka and mṛṣṭīkā (? are a great medicinal herb for the gods;
when combined with goat’s milk, it destroys diseases of the head.
One should cause [the patient] to drink equal parts of mango stone, dhātakī, and lodhra;
likewise, the leaves of the aśvattha tree destroy diarrhea.
Varuṇī combined with ghee and mixed with milk is the most excellent treatment for all locations within the female reproductive tract.
Mātuluṅga juice combined with rock salt is the most excellent treatment for all types of heart pain.
Sugar, licorice, and dhātrī; one type of soft earth that is red and painful;
ginger, sārivā, and likewise the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Having prepared Madhupuṣpa and Mṛṇāla, along with ghee and Pippalī,
one should cook oil with these together, adding four times the amount of milk.
Then, having removed [the heat], one should administer cold ghee followed by honey for cases of dyspnea,
cough, consumption, colic, heart disease, urinary disorders, and wounds.
In cases of jaundice, anemia, and severe obstructions,
as well as for the destruction of calamities caused by planets and serpents, [one should use] those which have been released.
A pregnant woman gives birth to a son who is wise and of radiant appearance;
this [medicine] should be administered to children to increase their strength and promote their growth.
If a woman performs this ritual for seven nights according to this procedure, she will [attain] women.
His diseases will perish, and many sons will be born to him.
Sandalwood, sārivā, rodhra, yaṣṭimadhu, utpala, kākolī,
kṣīrakākolī, and likewise kava and arddhī.
And he saw grapes, lotus stalks, chickpeas, and sugar.
Having collected all of these— vidārī, ikṣudaṇḍī, śatāvarī, and mahauṣadhi— one should have them ground into a fine paste.
The wise man should cook all these together into a single clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). By employing this entire preparation, one who desires sons shall obtain the status of a father of sons.
A pregnant woman gives birth to a wise and handsome son;
O lady of excellent vows, by merely drinking this while meditating, all [obstacles] are destroyed.
Clarified butter cooked with the juice of *mātuluṅga*,
parched grain flour, and rock salt destroys hiccup and asthma.
In her whose physical form does not tremble, yet who suffers from fever and pain in the heart,
as well as vomiting, delusion, labored breathing, and especially exhaustion;
Having recognized such a condition, one should perform this treatment for her:
*balā*, *atibalā*, *vṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*.
One should cook oil with these [substances] conjoined with Rohiṇī;
that is excellent for both as an ointment and for filling the ears.
This oil removes all diseases for pregnant women, without a doubt;
[it is prepared from] the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *paṇḍaka*, *āśvattha*, and *kapittha*.
Having collected these, one should boil them; thereafter, one should employ this bath. This bath, consisting of anointing and bathing, is indeed auspicious when performed.
This oil removes all diseases for pregnant women, without a doubt;
it may be taken with ghee, milk, food, or with the juice of mūdraka.
When this procedure is performed for women, they are liberated from diseases; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
For a woman who constantly suffers from disease and loses her embryo,
wholesome food consisting of soups, the juice of mūdraka beans, and meat-broths is beneficial.
Thus, by constantly employing [these means], she shall never suffer from disease;
she shall always be endowed with auspiciousness and ever speak kindly.
She is always compassionate, always devoted, always affectionate toward dharma, always desirous of her husband during his fertile season, and always moderate in her diet.
Having performed this very rite, one shall obtain all desires;
likewise, [one may use] the juice of *mātuluṅga*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *pippalī*.
One should drink [this] with white buttermilk; it is a destroyer of heart-pain, and during that period of discharge, it indeed brings about conception.
The wise should administer the root of *lāṅgalikā* together with honey; by applying it as an ointment to the navel, a woman gives birth with great ease.
One should combine the seeds of black gram with clarified butter;
having eaten them with milk and ghee, a woman will obtain a pregnancy.
If one takes a paste of pippalī, śṛṅgavera,
and keśara during the period of menstruation, even a woman who has borne only daughters will obtain a son.
Taking milk and rock salt along with ghee, O lady of a thousand smiles,
by merely drinking that, a woman will conceive a child.
One should grind eight seeds of *arjuna* with clarified butter and apply them as a mutual ointment; thus, she will give birth with ease.
To a newborn infant, one should cause this to be given as a linctus: ghee mixed with rock salt, [administered] during the Brahmāsāma days.
By this very [means], one becomes intelligent, illustrious, and of firm prowess;
powerful, handsome, and free from wrinkles and grey hair.
Dṛḍhasaṃdhi, Mahotsāha, Sahya, Udara, Parākrama,
Pipalī, Siṃdhava, Brāhmī, Suvarṇa, Varcālā, and Samī.
One should administer this as a linctus mixed with honey and clarified butter;
[the patient] will become strong, handsome, and free from wrinkles and grey hair.
"One who is intelligent and has many sons will undoubtedly obtain this linctus.
Lord Īśvara said:
Together with the planets, the Mothers, the world-protectors, and the Gaṇas,
I shall now describe in detail the sacrifice to the God of gods.
It is eight cubits in size, square, provided with four doors, and adorned;
upon it one should draw a lotus with filaments, beautiful in form.
Having prepared a seat according to the rule with the syllable Om,
one should worship the God in the pericarp;
then, one should assign the limbs to the body of Śiva.
One should worship the Mothers at the tips of the filaments, beginning with the north.
Īśānī should be worshipped in the north, Vaiṣṇavī [in the west], Brahmāṇī should be worshipped in the south, and one should worship Aindrī in the east.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Dhātrī, who is joined with her vehicles and accompanied by Āgneyī, Kaumārī, Vārāhī, and Naiṛtī.
In the center, however, one should perform the worship of the Kāmāras and the planets, starting from the east.
In the south, it is said that [the deity] Kaumāra is white; one should place Kaukika in the southwest (nairṛtya).
Apasmāra [is found] on the leaf of Vāruṇa; Viśākha is on * * * (?); [and] Pramehaka is on * * *.
The [mantras] beginning with the Heart and others are joined with their names and combined with the syllable *oṃ*;
preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*,
all follow the sequence of eight groups of eight, totaling sixty-four Mothers.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with the east;
one should worship the eight Gaṇas at the doors on the right side.
Āmardaka and Mahākāla, who are indeed terrifying, reside at the cremation ground, stationed at the southern and northern gates respectively.
In the west, one should worship Bhṛṅgirāṭ together with Dṛḍhakarṇa;
and at the eastern gate, one should worship Rauripiṅgala.
Kumbhakarṇa, Aśoka, Valabhojāta,
and Hāraka are joined respectively in the corners, starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast.
One should indeed worship these four planets in rites of fierce action;
furthermore, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) on the exterior, each in their own respective place.

The leader of practitioners, for the sake of protection within the mandala, should visualize [the deities] together with their own seed-syllables, joined with weapons, and accompanied by their retinues.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and likewise with food offerings;
having thus performed the worship, one should then bestow the consecration.
Now I shall explain another [rite] in the single-wheeled mandala;
having first placed Brahmāṇī and worshipped her according to the true rule.
O child, this group of nine, accompanied by Śiva, bestows success.
Whatever man constantly worships it according to this rite, [he shall attain his goal].
O virtuous one, accomplish everything that she desires to be done.
And for women who are to be executed, as well as for children afflicted by planetary influences—
one should worship with this [mantra] and then commence the ritual action.
Now, among the sixty-four [deities], whichever one might afflict a child,
starting from that *graha* and proceeding through the other eight in sequence—
Starting from the east and so forth, that [practitioner] should proceed with Śiva until the end;
having thus performed the ritual, each individual wheel is eightfold.
Having classified the modifications as types of action, medical treatment is indeed similar to that;
I shall describe each one of their life-sustaining principles in its entirety.
The Revatīs are known to be in the vehicle of the birds;
Pūtanā is said to be in the grain, but not in the seat of the Aśokas.
A woman has a seizure from a man; a sprout has a seizure from a seizure;
in the bath-water I have a seizure; in the hair-washing water, the cat has a seizure.
When food is served in broken vessels, the *jātahārikā* spirits arise;
the extremely fierce *dhruvagraha* seizes [the victim] by touching their limbs.
They fall with their husband as their death; one should not point out that they are swift from there.
Having been seized by men and enjoyed, the *bhāmaṇī* takes hold of the woman.
Sukra, Krodha, Mahākālī, and Bhañjaka are located in Puṣpavatī; Kesā is at Pauṇḍarīka, and the Grahi spirit Ṣaṣṭhikā is in the cremation ground.
While engaged in sexual intercourse, one should take the Pilipicchikās while weeping;
Mātṛnandā when there is indigestion, and Sunandā during thirsts.
The Māruta [is used] with *ūrdhvarevatī*; the *tṛc* [verses] are also [used] for water-sports;
likewise, Āryaka is used in walking, but not in sexual intercourse.
When the child sleeps during the day, or when it is cold, or when it is awake and seeks comfort,
these five— along with Śivā— seize the weeping infant.
At a crossroads for six months,
and in an empty house, the five planets always seize a neglected child.
Piṅgala seizes [the victim] upon one who has not bathed;
likewise, Setuka is seized at midday, and Bhīṣaṇa [seizes one] who is impure.
While weeping excessively, the prince seized the child;
and at the crossroads, Hrāsaka alone was captured by the fierce Śyena.
Kauśika, Avadhūta, and Apasmāra seize [the victim];
or whichever child is devoid of protection, Skandagraha seizes him.
When shaken by the wind, Prameha always seizes [the patient];
this has been declared as the individual life-span of each of the Grahas.
Mātṛnandā, Sunandā, and Revatī are the planetary spirits of the ancestors;
likewise are Āryakarā, Śītā, and Mukhamaṇḍī.
Indeed, these are the stealers of the fruit and flower of conception—
whosoever they may be— who have entered this mandala, the circle of the planets.
Those are the *grahas* (seizers), yet they seize; my commands, however, are the protectors.
Some are cruel, ever-greedy, difficult to conquer, and arrogant because of their strength.
But others, O Bhava, are incurable; they subsist on very little,
do not abandon pleasures, and are excluded from the mandala and the nine [initiations].
Whether it be a woman or a boy afflicted by a planet,
one should perform a maṇḍala for him as well as a propitiatory rite (śānti) for the planets.
If one should cause another to perform worship that has been taken up by someone else,
that person who performs the worship for another through a state of mental distortion will not be released from suffering.
Some [attain it] through bathing, decoctions, incenses, mustard seeds, or a sacred thread;
others through the rite of the mandala, and still others through the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya).
Having understood this and remaining in the proper place, one should then commence the ritual action;
the supreme mandala is to be drawn on the western side of a river.
To the left of the Mothers, one should draw the sacrificial fire situated in the southeast;
and in the center of the single tree that is the refuge of the world, one should likewise paint Jaśra.
First, at the beginning of the [direction] of Varuṇa (the west); then in a cremation ground by the Nairṛta (southwest);
likewise in an old well, according to one's desire, on a mountain, or at a crossroads.
To the northeast of a single linga, one should not plant groves or gardens;
to the south, four [should be made], and likewise to the north, one should draw eight squares of eight paces each.
On the southern side of the pond, one should draw the directions as desired;
in the northwest, the west, the center, and the cow-pen, one should draw the mandala.
One should draw [the design] at the confluence between the north and the northeast;
in the case of a pond, one should draw it on the southern side, or in any direction as desired.
These indeed are the positions there; those who have fallen from their positions due to defects will bring about fear, death, the destruction of the lineage, and poverty.
One's sons perish and the accomplishment of mantras does not arise.
Īśvara said:
Just as pleasure arises for women and young boys,
so too does a sensation arise within the embryo during its first month.
Equal parts of sandalwood, red lotus, ushira root,
and tagara should be ground with cold water, stirred with a clean finger, and administered to drink.
In this way, the fetus does not fall and her labor pains are pacified. || 1 ||
Then, in the second month, there arises a sensation within his embryo;
[the physician should prescribe] padmaka, bālaka, sṛṅgāṭa, and kiseruka.
Having ground these [drugs] with cold water and stirred them into thin milk, one should have her drink it;
thus the fetus will fall and the pain will be pacified. || 2 ||
Then, in the third month, there arises a sensation within his womb;
having taken lotus, sandalwood, and *śīra*, one should prepare them in equal proportions.
Having ground it with cold water and stirred it with milk, one should cause [the woman] to drink it;
thus the fetus will not fall, and that root [of the ailment] is pacified.
Then, in the fourth month of his gestation, there arises a sensation within the womb;
[one should take] padmaka, the root of the plantain tree, and blue utpala.
Having ground these with cold water and stirred them into milk, one should have her drink it;
thus the fetus will not fall and her pain will be pacified. || 4 ||
Then, in the fifth month of his gestation, there arises a sensation within the womb;
it is like a blue lotus with its root, and a kākolī plant with its stalk.
Having ground these with cold water and stirred them into milk, one should have [the woman] drink it.
In this way, the fetus will not be expelled, and her labor pains will be pacified. (5)
Then, in the sixth month of his gestation, there arises in the womb a sensation [like] that of a *piyāla* seed, a grape, and a blue lotus with its filaments.
Having ground these with cold water and stirred them in milk, one should have her drink it;
thus the fetus will not fall, and her labor pains will be pacified.
Then, in the seventh month of pregnancy, there arises a sensation;
[one should take] padmaka, hastipippalī, utpala, and dhanyaka in equal parts.
Having ground these with cold water and stirred them in milk, one should have her drink it;
thus the fetus will not fall and the labor pains will be pacified.
Then, in the eighth month, there arises a painful sensation regarding the fetus;
lotus, long pepper, blue water-lily, and coriander, taken in equal parts, destroy it.
Having ground these with cold water and mixed them with milk, one should have her drink it;
thus the fetus will not fall and the labor pains will be pacified. (8)
Then, in the ninth month, there arises a sensation within the womb;
[the remedy consists of] palāśa seeds, kākoli, and varuṇa, combined with roots.
Having steamed the fat until it is well-cooked, the wise man should consume it once it has digested;
in this way, the fetus will not fall and the labor pains will be pacified.
Then, in the tenth month, when he is in the womb, there arises a sensation;
[one should take] madhuka, padmaka, utpala, and vasanālaka.
One should grind these with cold water, dissolve them in milk, and have her drink it;
thus the fetus will not fall and the labor pains will be pacified.
And according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should first perform the ritual bathing as before.
Now, O daughter-in-law, I shall explain in brief, according to the truth and in accordance with the principles, the afflictions caused by the planets for children.
A woman who is like a crow, one who is barren, and likewise one whose children have died;
for such women joined with misfortune, the fetus is taken away from her.
In whatever manner these faults indeed arise,
I shall explain all of this out of my great affection for you, my son.
Those who repeatedly gaze at their own hair at crossroads,
at squares, and at the confluences of rivers;
If she is negligent while in an empty house, a temple, a family home, or during the twilight hours,
and is enjoyed by men who are not her own kin, then defects in the fetus will arise.
The neck was broken across, saliva flowed from the mouth,
his limbs trembled, and he had no desire for food.
The planet named Pāvanī grasps the newborn;
one should perform for that child the remedial treatment of medical therapy.
With mañjiṣṭhā, dhātakī, rodhra, haritāla, and sandalwood—
by means of this, that possessed person releases the spirit from the liṅga.
Having given a portion to the Mothers at all times, the wise man [should offer] perfume,
garlands, liquor, meat, cooked food, and meat according to his desire.
O child, when this alone is performed, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Furthermore, the body certainly trembles and its limbs contract.
That seizure named Bhīṣaṇī seizes for two nights;
[the remedy consists of] Apāmārga, Suśira, Pippalī, and likewise Citraka.
Having ground these with goat's milk, one should then wash the hair;
one should fumigate it with a cow's horn using *naivaka* wood together with nails.
Having given a portion to the Mothers, he then releases the child.
He yawns and stretches again and again on his iron bed;
he opens his eyes, yet food does not please him.
One should take that Ghaṇṭālī and recite its name for three nights.
Then, having ground elephant tusk and cow tusk with goat’s milk, one should smear the hair [of the child] with it.
One should fumigate [the area] with neem leaves and husks mixed with mustard seeds.
Whether it has been fumigated or smeared with ointment, she who possesses it will release it from there.
He raises his hood, casts his gaze toward the quarters of the sky,
agitates his limbs, and weeps again and again.
One should take Kākoli, recite its name for three nights,
and combine it with elephant tusk, snake-skin, and mustard seeds.
Having ground these with cow urine, one should then smear the hair;
one should fumigate it with mustard seeds and neem leaves.
Having given a portion to the Mothers, he then releases the child.
The fool who has entered into the assembly constantly clenches his fist.
She yawns, makes sounds, and gazes at food;
she is the female spirit named Grahī, who seizes for five nights.
Having ground together in a single portion of water the horn of a ram, *vaya*, *rodhra*, yellow orpiment, and realgar, one should then apply that paste to the hair.
Having given a portion to the Mothers, that possessing spirit then releases [the victim];
it strikes at the hands and feet and laughs again and again.
The child weeps or becomes delirious, and food no longer appeals to him;
that spirit named Phetkārī seizes him for a period of six nights.
Having ground together guggulu, kuṣṭha, vairāja, and mustard seeds,
and having mixed them with the ashes of a corpse, one should then smear it upon the hair.
Having given a portion to the Mothers, that seizing spirit then releases her.
Having seized it, he does not let go his cry but wails constantly like a crow;
moreover, a foul odor arises from the hair, of this there is no doubt.
One with loose hair is seized by the spirit named Grahi for seven nights;
one should grind kuṣṭha and white fat together with cow’s urine.
The child should be anointed with these and burned as incense with *vyāghranakha*;
having offered a portion to the Mothers, he is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (7)
The infant cries out excessively while becoming bewildered;
he gazes toward the quarters and constantly lolls his tongue.
That [fever] is called *grahī*; one should administer a plaster (*pralepa*) made from the roots of *vacā* and *hiṅgu*, along with honey and clarified butter (*sarpis*), for eight nights.
Having given a portion to the Mothers, one is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
The child trembles again and again, breathes repeatedly,
cries out, becomes pale, and clenches both his fists.
One should not seize a goat or a sheep, nor accept a triple-strand necklace;
likewise, [one should avoid] vacha, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, tagara, and white mustard seeds.
Having ground these with water, one should then smear them upon the hair;
or likewise, O man, one may use incense together with human nails for the sake of curing diseases.
Having given a portion to the Mothers according to her desire through meditative absorption (samādhi),
the seizer then releases the child who has been smeared or fumigated.
The child has a complexion like the hue of a blue lotus;
he cries by day and night, yet sleeps with a fragrant scent.
That seizing [fever] named Rodanī seizes one for ten nights;
[the remedy consists of] kuṣṭha, sarja, sañca, vacā, and mustard seeds.
Having ground these with water, one should then smear the hair;
for the incense, use neem leaves together with *māṃsī* and lac.
One should give a portion of cooked rice mixed with *asanaka* and *kodrava* to the Mothers;
however, for a child born within ten nights, medical treatment should be administered.
Above [the ground], one should smear each individual Mother in her own form, one by one in sequence, for a month at a time, or for a year, or even beyond that.
Thus ends the chapter on the medical treatment of infants immediately after birth in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, listen to the treatment for children born in the various months;
the Pūtanās and Śakunis seize those born in the [respective] months.
As soon as it is seized by her, it emits the cry of a crow;
it cries out day and night, and the stench of a vulture arises.
When blood is heard [in the ears], one no longer sees with the eyes;
therefore, O Sāramati, Pūtanā constantly desires the row of eyes.
One should offer three kinds of milk-rice (pāyasa) and likewise four kinds of meat;

Now, therefore, I shall explain the characteristics of the *sākinīs*:
Māheśvarī, Brāhmī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.

she should be known as a *sākinī*, who is beautiful when alone at night.

never leaves a mark upon the ground by her new footsteps.
That woman should be known as a *sākinī* by the foremost of practitioners at all times;

One should offer an oblation of meat and fumigate with flowers and perfumes;

One should employ the third letter of the fourth class, ignited by fire and wind— that is, the letter *ja* endowed with the *bindu*— at the time of the *stobha*.
That very [breath], conjoined with the wind, should be made to pierce the sound of a youth;
one should not speak constantly in that manner, nor should there be running or leaping.
The letter *la* is situated in the Mahendra [square], located in the middle of the city;
it is yellow and surmounted by a bindu, and one should employ it at the time of union.
One should contemplate that divine syllable *ya*, mounted upon the bindu and preceded by a half-moon, which effects nourishment, as a rain shower upon the crown of the head.

the practitioners of the Yoginīs must not allow [the essence] to exit.
The *sākinīs* become angry with him and his mantra-attainment is destroyed;
one should always perform their worship with ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and they will release him.
